items.label: Psalm 1
items.title: The Two Ways
items.html:
Psalm 1

The Two Ways

1 How blessed1 is the man2
 who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked,
 and in the way of sinners has not stood,
 and in the seat of mockers has not sat!
2 Rather,3 in the law4 of the LORD is his delight,
 and on His law he meditates5 by day and by night.
3 He shall be like a tree transplanted6 beside channels7 of water,
 which gives its fruit in its season,
 and its leaf does not wither;
 and in all that he does, he prospers.8
4 Not so the wicked!
 Instead9 they are like the chaff
 that the wind drives away.
5 Therefore the wicked will not rise10 in the judgment,
 nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.
6 For the LORD knows11 the way of the righteous,
 but the way of the wicked shall perish.

  1. Heb ʾashre, an exclamatory plural construct, lit. O the blessednesses of; or How happy. It is a different word from baruk, “blessed.” ↩

  2. Heb ʾish, a singular man. The statement applies to anyone who lives this way (or the one). ↩

  3. Heb ki ʾim, a strong adversative after a negative: but rather. ↩

  4. Heb torah, lit. instruction, teaching: the LORD’s direction for life, not only legal statutes. The same word occurs both times in this verse. ↩

  5. Or murmurs, ponders aloud. Heb hagah can denote low vocal sound. ↩

  6. Heb shatul, which is used of something deliberately planted (set out by a cultivator) rather than growing wild. Or planted. ↩

  7. Or streams. Heb palge mayim likely refers to irrigation channels. ↩

  8. Or and all that he does prospers. The subject of the Hebrew verb is ambiguous (some take it as the tree: all that it produces prospers). ↩

  9. Heb ki ʾim, as in v. 2. ↩

  10. Or stand, stand up. That is, they will not be able to hold their ground (qum). ↩

  11. Heb participle, is knowing. Or watches over, cares for. Hebrew “to know” often implies close, personal regard (cf. Amos 3:2). ↩

items.label: Psalm 2
items.title: The LORD's Anointed King
items.html:
Psalm 2

The LORD’s Anointed King

1 Why are the nations in an uproar,1
 and the peoples murmuring2 what is empty?
2 The kings of the earth take their stand,
 and the rulers have conspired3 together
 against the LORD and against His Anointed:4
3 “Let us tear apart their bonds,
 and cast away their cords from us!”
4 He who sits5 in the heavens laughs;
 the Lord6 holds them in derision.
5 Then He will speak to them in His anger,
 and in His burning wrath He will terrify them:
6 “But as for Me, I have installed7 My king
 upon Zion, My holy mountain.”
7 I will tell of8 the decree:
 the LORD said to me, “You are My son;
 today I have begotten you.
8 Ask of Me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance,
 and as your possession the ends of the earth.
9 You shall shatter9 them with a rod of iron;
 like a potter’s vessel you shall dash them to pieces.”
10 So now, O kings, show insight;
 accept correction,10 you judges of the earth.
11 Serve the LORD with fear,
 and rejoice with trembling.
12 Kiss the son,11 lest He12 be angry and you perish in the way,13
 for His anger is quickly14 kindled.
 How blessed15 are all who take refuge in Him!

  1. Heb ragheshu. This is the only place the verb occurs. It means to be in commotion, throng tumultuously. ↩

  2. Heb hagah, the same verb rendered “meditates” in Ps 1:2. It contrasts deliberately with that verse: the righteous murmur the LORD’s law, while the nations murmur emptiness. ↩

  3. Heb nosedu, lit. have sat together, taken counsel together. ↩

  4. Heb meshiḥo, His anointed one (cf. “messiah”). ↩

  5. Or is enthroned. ↩

  6. Heb ʾAdonay. ↩

  7. Heb nasakhti. This root usually means pour out (a libation), but here it is generally understood as install, set (perhaps from a homonymous root, or with reference to anointing). LXX reads But I was appointed king by Him on Zion, His holy mountain, which makes the king the speaker. ↩

  8. Lit. I will recount concerning. The anointed king is now the speaker. ↩

  9. MT teroʿem, you shall break them (from raʿaʿ). LXX and Syriac read you shall shepherd them (tirʿem, from raʿah), which uses the same consonants with different vowels; cf. Rev 2:27; 12:5; 19:15. ↩

  10. Or be warned, be instructed. Heb hiwwaseru (Niphal of yasar, “discipline, instruct”). ↩

  11. Heb nashshequ bar. Bar is the Aramaic word for son; v. 7 uses the Hebrew ben. Hebrew bar also means pure, so some render kiss sincerely or worship in purity (thus Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew). LXX reads Take hold of instruction, and the Targum reads Receive instruction. Some scholars emend vv. 11b–12a to with trembling kiss His feet. Kissing as an act of homage to a king is attested (cf. 1 Sam 10:1; 1 Kgs 19:18). ↩

  12. Or he, i.e., the son. The Hebrew pronoun could refer to the LORD or to the son. ↩

  13. Or perish from the way. Lit. perish way. Compare the way that perishes in Ps 1:6. ↩

  14. Or soon, easily. Heb kimʿat. ↩

  15. Heb ʾashre, as in Ps 1:1. Together the two verses frame Psalms 1–2 as a pair. ↩

items.label: Psalm 3
items.title: Morning Trust Amid Many Foes
items.html:
Psalm 3

Morning Trust Amid Many Foes

A Psalm1 of David,2 when he fled from Absalom his son.

13 O LORD, how numerous my adversaries have become!
 Many are rising up against me.
2 Many are saying of my soul,4
 “There is no salvation for him in God.”
Selah5
3 But You, O LORD, are a shield about me,
 my glory, and the One who lifts up my head.
4 With my voice I cried6 to the LORD,
 and He answered me from His holy mountain.
Selah
5 I lay down and slept;
 I awoke, for the LORD sustains me.
6 I will not be afraid of myriads of people
 who have set themselves against me all around.
7 Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!
 For You have struck7 all my enemies on the jaw;
 the teeth of the wicked You have shattered.
8 Salvation is the LORD’s;
 upon Your people be Your blessing!
Selah

  1. Heb mizmor, a song, probably one sung with instrumental accompaniment (from zamar, “sing, make music”). ↩

  2. Heb le-David: of, by, for, or belonging to David. The same applies throughout. ↩

  3. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–8 in English are vv. 2–9 in Hebrew. ↩

  4. Heb nephesh. Or of me. ↩

  5. A liturgical or musical term of uncertain meaning. It occurs 71 times in Psalms and 3 times in Habakkuk 3. ↩

  6. Heb imperfect followed by a wayyiqtol (narrative past) form. Or I cry … and He answers. ↩

  7. Or, read as a prayer: Strike … shatter. Some take these perfects as precative. ↩

items.label: Psalm 4
items.title: Peace in the Night
items.html:
Psalm 4

Peace in the Night

For the director;1 with stringed instruments.2 A Psalm of David.

13 When I call, answer me, O God of my righteousness!
 In distress You have made room for me;4
 be gracious to me, and hear my prayer.
2 O sons of men,5 how long shall my glory become a disgrace?
 How long will you love what is empty, and seek after falsehood?
Selah
3 But know that the LORD has set apart6 the godly one7 for Himself;
 the LORD hears when I call to Him.
4 Tremble,8 and do not sin;
 speak in your heart upon your bed, and be silent.
Selah
5 Offer sacrifices of righteousness,
 and trust in the LORD.
6 Many are saying, “Who will show us any good?”
 Lift up9 the light of Your face upon us, O LORD.
7 You have put gladness in my heart,
 more than when10 their grain and their new wine abound.
8 In peace I will both lie down and sleep,
 for You alone,11 O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

  1. Heb la-menatstseaḥ, probably for the leader of the temple music. The meaning is debated. ↩

  2. Heb bi-neginot. ↩

  3. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–8 in English are vv. 2–9 in Hebrew. ↩

  4. Lit. You have made wide for me. This is an image of release from a narrow, constricting place (Heb tsar, “distress,” is related to “narrow”). ↩

  5. Heb bene ʾish. This may mean men of rank, in contrast to bene ʾadam (cf. Ps 49:2; 62:9). ↩

  6. Heb hiphlah, has distinguished, set apart. Some interpreters emend to hiphliʾ ḥasdo, has shown wonderful lovingkindness (cf. Ps 31:21). ↩

  7. Heb ḥasid, one who is loyal to the LORD’s covenant love (ḥesed). ↩

  8. Or Be agitated, Be angry. Heb rigzu. LXX reads Be angry and do not sin, a reading quoted in Eph 4:26. ↩

  9. Heb nesah, an unusual form, generally taken as from nasaʾ, lift up (cf. Num 6:26). ↩

  10. Lit. from the time. ↩

  11. Heb le-vadad, alone, in isolation. It may describe the LORD (You alone) or the psalmist’s safety (make me dwell alone, in safety; cf. Deut 33:28). ↩

items.label: Psalm 5
items.title: A Morning Prayer for Guidance
items.html:
Psalm 5

A Morning Prayer for Guidance

For the director; for the flutes.1 A Psalm of David.

12 Give ear to my words, O LORD;
 consider my sighing.3
2 Attend to the sound of my cry for help,
 my King and my God,
 for to You I pray.
3 O LORD, in the morning You will hear my voice;
 in the morning I will lay out my case4 before You, and keep watch.
4 For You are not a God who delights in wickedness;
 evil5 may not dwell with You.
5 The boastful will not take their stand before Your eyes;
 You hate all who work iniquity.6
6 You destroy those who speak a lie;
 the LORD abhors a man of bloodshed7 and deceit.
7 But as for me, through the abundance of Your lovingkindness8 I will enter Your house;
 I will bow down toward Your holy temple in fear of You.
8 O LORD, lead me in Your righteousness because of those who watch for me;9
 make Your way straight10 before me.
9 For there is nothing reliable in their mouth;11
 their inward part is destruction;
 their throat is an open grave;
 they make their tongue smooth.
10 Hold them guilty, O God;
 let them fall by their own counsels;
 in the multitude of their transgressions drive them away,
 for they have rebelled against You.
11 But let all who take refuge in You be glad;
 let them shout for joy forever;
 and may You shelter them,
 that those who love Your name may exult in You.
12 For You bless the righteous, O LORD;
 You surround him with favor as with a shield.12

  1. Heb ʾel-ha-neḥilot. The meaning is uncertain: possibly for flutes or the name of a tune. ↩

  2. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–12 in English are vv. 2–13 in Hebrew. ↩

  3. Or murmuring, meditation. Heb hagig, which is related to hagah (Ps 1:2). It occurs only here and in Ps 39:3. ↩

  4. Heb ʾeʿerakh, I will set in order, arrange. The verb is used for laying out a sacrifice (Lev 1:7–8) and for laying out a legal case (Job 23:4). The object is unstated. ↩

  5. Or an evil person. Lit. evil will not sojourn with You. ↩

  6. Heb ʾawen, wickedness, trouble. ↩

  7. Lit. bloods. ↩

  8. Heb ḥesed: loyal, covenant love. ↩

  9. Heb shoreray, those who watch me (with hostility). ↩

  10. Ketiv (the written consonants) hoshar; Qere (the reading tradition) hayshar. Both are Hiphil imperatives of yashar, make straight, so the meaning is the same. ↩

  11. Lit. his mouth. The singular is distributive: each of them. Vv. 9b–c are quoted in Rom 3:13. ↩

  12. Heb tsinnah, a large shield that covers the whole body. ↩

items.label: Psalm 6
items.title: A Plea for Mercy in Distress
items.html:
Psalm 6

A Plea for Mercy in Distress

For the director; with stringed instruments; upon the Sheminith.1 A Psalm of David.

12 O LORD, do not in Your anger rebuke me,
 nor in Your wrath discipline me.
2 Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am withering away;
 heal me, O LORD, for my bones are dismayed.3
3 And my soul4 is greatly dismayed;
 but You,5 O LORD—how long?
4 Return, O LORD, rescue my soul;
 save me for the sake of Your lovingkindness.6
5 For in death there is no remembrance of You;
 in Sheol who will give You thanks?
6 I am weary with my groaning;
 every night I make my bed swim;7
 with my tears I drench my couch.
7 My eye wastes away because of grief;
 it grows old because of all my foes.
8 Depart from me, all you who work iniquity,
 for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.
9 The LORD has heard my plea for grace;
 the LORD accepts my prayer.
10 All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly dismayed;8
 they shall turn back, they shall be ashamed in a moment.

  1. Lit. the eighth. This may refer to an eight-stringed instrument or to a lower octave. The meaning is uncertain. ↩

  2. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–10 in English are vv. 2–11 in Hebrew. ↩

  3. Heb nivhalu, are terrified, dismayed. The same verb (bahal) occurs in vv. 3 and 10 and is rendered the same way each time, so the reader can follow the reversal: the psalmist’s dismay passes to the enemies. ↩

  4. Heb nephesh. ↩

  5. Ketiv ʾat (an unusual form spelled like the feminine you); Qere ʾattah. ↩

  6. Heb ḥesed: loyal, covenant love. ↩

  7. Heb ʾasḥeh, lit. cause to swim, i.e., flood. ↩

  8. Or Let all my enemies be ashamed … The forms can be read as jussive (a wish). ↩

items.label: Psalm 7
items.title: The Righteous Judge
items.html:
Psalm 7

The Righteous Judge

A Shiggaion1 of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite.2

13 O LORD my God, in You I have taken refuge;
 save me from all who pursue me, and deliver me,
2 lest he tear my soul like a lion,
 dragging me away, with no one to deliver.
3 O LORD my God, if I have done this,
 if there is injustice in my hands,
4 if I have repaid with evil the one at peace with me,4
 or have plundered5 my adversary without cause,
5 let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it;
 let him trample my life to the ground,
 and lay my glory6 in the dust.
Selah
6 Arise, O LORD, in Your anger;
 lift Yourself up against the fury of my foes,
 and awake for me;7 You have commanded judgment.
7 Let the assembly of the peoples gather around You,
 and over it return8 on high.
8 The LORD judges the peoples;
 judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness,
 and according to the integrity that is in me.
9 Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end,
 but establish the righteous;
 for the One who tests hearts and minds9 is the righteous God.
10 My shield rests with God,10
 who saves the upright in heart.
11 God is a righteous judge,
 and a God who shows indignation every day.
12 If a man11 does not turn back, He will sharpen His sword;
 He has bent His bow and made it ready.
13 He has prepared for Himself the weapons of death;
 He makes His arrows into flaming shafts.
14 Behold, he is in labor with iniquity;
 he has conceived trouble and given birth to falsehood.
15 He has dug a pit and hollowed it out,
 and has fallen into the hole he was making.
16 His trouble returns upon his own head,
 and upon his own crown his violence comes down.
17 I will give thanks to the LORD according to His righteousness,
 and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High.

  1. Heb shiggayon. The meaning is uncertain; it is perhaps a lament or an impassioned song (cf. the plural in Hab 3:1). ↩

  2. Heb ben-yemini. Cush is not otherwise known. ↩

  3. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–17 in English are vv. 2–18 in Hebrew. ↩

  4. Heb sholmi, my ally, the one at peace with me. ↩

  5. Heb waʾaḥalletsah. Elsewhere this Piel verb usually means rescue. That has led some to read a parenthesis: (rather, I rescued the one who was my adversary without cause). The rendering here follows those who see a sense like strip, plunder (compare the related noun in 2 Sam 2:21 and Judg 14:19). ↩

  6. Or my honor. Some suggest my liver, i.e., my inner self (reading kavedi; cf. Gen 49:6). ↩

  7. LXX reads O LORD my God (reading ʾelohay for ʾelay). ↩

  8. Some propose reading shevah, be seated (enthroned), for MT shuvah, return. ↩

  9. Lit. hearts and kidneys. In Hebrew the kidneys stand for the innermost thoughts and emotions. ↩

  10. Lit. My shield is upon God, i.e., God is the one who bears my shield. ↩

  11. Lit. If he does not turn. The subject is unstated. It may be the unrepentant man (as here), or the sentence may read Surely he (the wicked) will again sharpen his sword. In that reading the weapons of vv. 12–13 belong to the wicked, which leads into vv. 14–16. ↩

items.label: Psalm 8
items.title: The Majesty of God's Name and the Dignity of Man
items.html:
Psalm 8

The Majesty of God’s Name and the Dignity of Man

For the director; upon the Gittith.1 A Psalm of David.

12 O LORD, our Lord,3
 how magnificent is Your name in all the earth,
 You who have set4 Your splendor above the heavens!
2 From the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have founded strength5
 because of Your adversaries,
 to silence the enemy and the avenger.
3 When I look at Your heavens, the work of Your fingers,
 the moon and the stars, which You have set in place,
4 what is man,6 that You remember him,
 and the son of man,7 that You attend to him?
5 Yet You have made him a little lower than God,8
 and with glory and honor You crown him.
6 You make him ruler over the works of Your hands;
 all things You have put under his feet,
7 sheep and oxen, all of them,
 and also the beasts of the field,
8 the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea,
 whatever passes along the paths of the seas.
9 O LORD, our Lord,
 how magnificent is Your name in all the earth!

  1. Heb ha-gittit. The meaning is uncertain. It may be an instrument or tune associated with Gath, or connected with gat, “winepress.” ↩

  2. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–9 in English are vv. 2–10 in Hebrew. ↩

  3. Heb YHWH ʾadonenu. ↩

  4. Heb ʾasher tenah is difficult. Tenah looks like an imperative (set!). Many read natattah, You have set. LXX reads for Your magnificence is lifted up above the heavens. ↩

  5. Or a stronghold. LXX reads You have prepared praise, the form quoted in Matt 21:16. ↩

  6. Heb ʾenosh, mortal man. ↩

  7. Heb ben-ʾadam, a human being. Cf. Heb 2:6–8. ↩

  8. Heb ʾelohim. Or the heavenly beings. LXX reads angels, quoted in Heb 2:7. Lit. You have made him lack a little from God. ↩

items.label: Psalm 9
items.title: Thanksgiving to the Judge of the Nations
items.html:
Psalm 9

Thanksgiving to the Judge of the Nations

For the director; upon Muth-labben.1 A Psalm of David.2

א Aleph

13 I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart;
 I will recount all Your wonderful deeds.
2 I will be glad and exult in You;
 I will sing praise to Your name, O Most High.

ב Bet

3 When my enemies turn back,
 they stumble and perish before You.
4 For You have upheld my just claim and my cause;4
 You have sat on the throne, judging righteously.

ג Gimel

5 You have rebuked the nations; You have destroyed the wicked;
 their name You have blotted out forever and ever.
6 The enemy has come to an end in everlasting ruins;
 their cities You have uprooted;
 the very memory of them has perished.5
7 But the LORD sits enthroned forever;
 He has established His throne for judgment,
8 and He Himself will judge the world in righteousness;
 He will execute judgment for the peoples with equity.
9 May the LORD be a high refuge6 for the oppressed,
 a high refuge in times of trouble.
10 And those who know Your name will trust in You,
 for You, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek You.

ז Zayin

11 Sing praises to the LORD, who dwells in Zion!
 Declare among the peoples His deeds!
12 For He who requires blood7 remembers them;
 He does not forget the cry of the afflicted.8

ח Ḥet

13 Be gracious to me, O LORD!
 See my affliction from those who hate me,
 You who lift me up from the gates of death,
14 that I may recount all Your praises
 in the gates of the daughter of Zion;
 I will rejoice in Your salvation.

ט Tet

15 The nations have sunk down into the pit they made;
 in the net which they hid their own foot has been caught.
16 The LORD has made Himself known; He has executed judgment;
 the wicked is snared9 in the work of his own hands.
Higgaion.10 Selah

י Yod

17 The wicked shall return to Sheol,
 all the nations that forget God.

כ Kaph

18 For the needy shall not always be forgotten,
 nor shall the hope of the afflicted11 perish forever.
19 Arise, O LORD! Do not let man12 prevail;
 let the nations be judged before You.
20 Put them in fear,13 O LORD;
 let the nations know they are but men.
Selah

  1. Heb ʿal-mut labben, lit. upon death, for the son. It is probably the name of a tune; the meaning is uncertain. Some propose reading ʿal ʿalamot (cf. Ps 46 superscription). LXX reads concerning the hidden things of the son. ↩

  2. Psalms 9 and 10. Together these form a single, incomplete alphabetic acrostic. In this edition the Hebrew letters mark stanzas only where the acrostic is clear.
    - The acrostic: It runs from aleph to kaph in Ps 9, with dalet missing and he–vav irregular in vv. 6–10. Lamed opens Ps 10:1. After that the sequence is disrupted until qof, resh, shin, and tav, which close the poem (10:12–18).
    - Unity: Ps 10 has no superscription, which is unusual in Book I. LXX and the Vulgate treat 9–10 as one psalm, which is why their numbering runs one behind the Hebrew from Ps 10 through Ps 147. The two psalms also share vocabulary, e.g., in times of trouble (9:9; 10:1), Arise, O LORD (9:19; 10:12), man (ʾenosh, 9:19–20; 10:18), and the afflicted. ↩

  3. In Hebrew the superscription is v. 1, so vv. 1–20 in English are vv. 2–21 in Hebrew. ↩

  4. Lit. You have done my judgment and my cause. ↩

  5. The Hebrew of v. 6 is difficult. Lit. The enemy—they are finished, ruins forever; and cities You uprooted; their memory perished, they. The final hemmah, they, is sometimes repointed or joined to v. 7. ↩

  6. Heb misgav, a secure height or stronghold. ↩

  7. I.e., He avenges bloodshed (cf. Gen 9:5). ↩

  8. Ketiv ʿaniyyim, afflicted; Qere ʿanawim, humble. The two terms overlap and are often interchanged by Ketiv/Qere in Psalms. ↩

  9. MT noqesh, pointed as an active participle: He (the LORD) snares the wicked. LXX and many interpreters read noqash, is snared. ↩

  10. Heb higgayon, probably a musical or liturgical notation, related to hagah (cf. Ps 1:2; 92:3). ↩

  11. Ketiv ʿanawim, humble; Qere ʿaniyyim, afflicted. The negative of the first line governs both lines in Hebrew. ↩

  12. Heb ʾenosh, mortal man. ↩

  13. MT morah, fear (or perhaps a variant spelling of moraʾ, terror). LXX reads Appoint a lawgiver over them (reading moreh, teacher). ↩

items.label: Psalm 10
items.title: Why Do You Stand Far Off?[^1]
items.html:
Psalm 10

Why Do You Stand Far Off?1

ל Lamed

1 Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?
 Why do You hide Yourself in times of trouble?
2 In arrogance the wicked hotly pursues the afflicted;
 let them be caught2 in the schemes which they have devised.
3 For the wicked boasts of the desire of his soul,
 and the greedy man blesses3—he spurns the LORD.
4 The wicked, in the height of his nose,4 does not seek Him;
 all his schemes are, “There is no God.”
5 His ways endure5 at all times;
 Your judgments are on high, out of his sight;
 as for all his foes, he snorts at them.
6 He says in his heart, “I shall not be moved;
 through generation after generation I shall not be in adversity.”6
7 His mouth is full of cursing, and deceit, and oppression;7
 under his tongue are trouble and iniquity.
8 He sits in ambush in the villages;
 in hiding places he kills the innocent;
 his eyes stealthily watch for the helpless.8
9 He lies in wait in a hiding place, like a lion in his thicket;
 he lies in wait to seize the afflicted;
 he seizes the afflicted when he draws him into his net.
10 He crushes, he crouches low,
 and the helpless fall by his might.9
11 He says in his heart, “God has forgotten;
 He has hidden His face; He will never see.”

ק Qof

12 Arise, O LORD! O God, lift up Your hand!
 Do not forget the humble.10
13 Why has the wicked spurned God?
 He has said in his heart, “You will not require it.”

ר Resh

14 You have seen it, for You look upon trouble and vexation,
 to take it into Your hand.
 The helpless commits himself to You;
 You have been the helper of the fatherless.

ש Shin

15 Break the arm of the wicked and the evil man;
 seek out his wickedness until You find none.11
16 The LORD is King forever and ever;
 the nations have perished from His land.

ת Tav

17 The desire of the humble You have heard, O LORD;
 You will strengthen their heart; You will incline Your ear
18 to vindicate the fatherless and the oppressed,
 so that man,12 who is of the earth, may terrify no more.

  1. Ps 10 has no superscription. On its probable unity with Ps 9 and the shared acrostic, see the note on the Ps 9 superscription. The Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same here. In LXX and the Vulgate, Ps 10 is part of Ps 9 (9:22–39). ↩

  2. Or they (the afflicted) are caught. The subject is ambiguous. ↩

  3. Heb berekh, blesses. The line is difficult. Some take blesses as a euphemism for curses (as in Job 1:5; 1 Kgs 21:10, 13): the greedy man curses and spurns the LORD. Others read he blesses the greedy, he spurns the LORD. ↩

  4. I.e., in his pride. ↩

  5. Heb yaḥilu. The meaning here is uncertain; it is perhaps are firm, prosper. Ketiv darko, his way; Qere derakhaw, his ways. ↩

  6. Lit. to generation and generation, who not in evil. Some scholars join the final words to the first word of v. 7 (ʾalah, cursing). ↩

  7. V. 7a is quoted in Rom 3:14. ↩

  8. Heb ḥelkah, a rare word found only in this psalm (vv. 8, 14; cf. v. 10 Ketiv). The meaning is uncertain: the hapless, the unfortunate. ↩

  9. The Hebrew of v. 10 is difficult. Ketiv wedakah, Qere yidkeh (he crushes or is crushed). Ketiv ḥelkaʾim (hapless ones), Qere ḥel kaʾim (a host of the dejected). By his might is lit. by his strong ones, perhaps his claws. ↩

  10. Ketiv ʿaniyyim, afflicted; Qere ʿanawim, humble. ↩

  11. Lit. You will not find. ↩

  12. Heb ʾenosh, mortal man. ↩

items.title: Translation style guide
items.html:
Style Guide: An Original Essentially-Literal Translation (working title)

1. Aim

Translate afresh from the original languages. Use the NASB’s philosophy as the base (formal equivalence, word-level accountability, consistent key terms, supplied words marked) and the ESV’s as the polish (essentially literal, dignified, readable literary English). No wording is copied or closely paraphrased from the NASB, ESV, or any other copyrighted version. Where a rendering lines up with theirs, that happens only because the Hebrew allows one natural English rendering. In those cases, compare against the public-domain tradition (KJV/ASV) and the Hebrew, never against the NASB or ESV.

2. Source texts

  • OT: Masoretic Text as found in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC), using the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB) morphology and Strong’s-keyed lemmas (github.com/openscriptures/morphhb). File used for Psalms: wlc/Ps.xml.
  • Versions consulted only for textual questions: LXX, Dead Sea Scrolls, Syriac, Vulgate. These are cited in footnotes, never adopted silently.
  • NT (later): a critical Greek text with an open license (e.g., SBLGNT or a comparable openly licensed edition). To be decided when we reach the NT.

3. Formal vs. readable: the balance rules

  1. The default is formal. Keep Hebrew word order, imagery, idiom, and the parallel structure of lines whenever the English can still be read.
  2. Smooth only when the literal English would be wrong, misleading, or ungrammatical. When we smooth, put the literal sense in a footnote (Lit.).
  3. Each English word is accountable to the source. Do not expand or interpret in the text itself. Commentary goes in footnotes only.
  4. Respect the verb forms. Render qatal/perfect, yiqtol/imperfect, and participles with care. If a form is ambiguous in poetry, choose the most natural English and give the alternative in a footnote.
  5. Use literary but current English. No “thee/thou.” Avoid slang and contractions. Prefer concrete words to abstract ones.
  6. Gender language: keep the singular masculine of the Hebrew (ʾish = “man”) where the text has it. When the sense is generic, add a footnote (“or the one”).

4. The divine name and divine titles

Hebrew Rendering
YHWH (יהוה) LORD (small caps; written LORD in markdown)
ʾAdonay Lord
ʾAdonay YHWH Lord GOD
ʾElohim (of the true God) God
ʾEl God (footnote “Heb El” where the distinction matters)
ʿElyon Most High
YHWH Tsevaʾot LORD of hosts
Yah LORD (footnote “Heb Yah”); keep Hallelu-Yah as “Praise the LORD” with a footnote

Pronouns referring to God are capitalized (He, His, Him, You, Your). This follows NASB practice. Where it is unclear whether the referent is God, use lowercase and add a footnote.

5. Supplied words

  • Words that have no direct counterpart in the source but are needed for English sense go in italics (markdown *word*). The verbless copula (“is,” “are”) counts as supplied.
  • Use [square brackets] only for text whose originality is doubtful (textual variants).
  • Do not italicize ordinary function words that are already implied by Hebrew grammar (articles, prepositions folded into a verb, the object marker, etc.).

6. Footnotes

Footnotes are numbered per chapter in markdown ([^1]). They use these labels: - Lit.: the woodenly literal Hebrew sense. - Or: a legitimate alternative rendering. - Heb: the transliterated Hebrew term, used when the word itself matters. - MT / LXX / DSS / Syr / Vg: textual notes, which give the reading adopted and the alternatives. - Cf.: a cross-reference to a parallel passage, used sparingly. Keep footnotes factual and short. No devotional commentary.

7. Hebrew poetry layout

  • Each verse begins with a bold verse number.
  • One line per Hebrew colon. The first colon of a verse sits at the margin, and the second and third cola are indented two spaces. Cola are divided according to the Masoretic accents (ʾatnaḥ, ʿole weyored, etc.).
  • Keep the parallelism visible. Do not merge cola.
  • Mark acrostic psalms (e.g., 9–10, 25, 34, 111, 112, 119, 145) with the Hebrew letter at the head of each stanza.

8. Superscriptions and Selah

  • Superscriptions are canonical text in the MT, where they count as verse 1 (or as vv. 1–2). Print them in italics before the psalm body. Use English verse numbering and note the Hebrew numbering in a footnote at the first verse affected.
  • Technical terms whose meaning is uncertain (miktam, maskil, shiggaion, ʿal-hashsheminit, etc.) are transliterated, with a footnote that gives the probable sense or says “meaning uncertain.”
  • Selah is kept as Selah. It is set right-aligned or on its own line, and its first occurrence (Ps 3:2) gets a footnote saying “a liturgical or musical term of uncertain meaning.”

8a. Editorial headings

Each psalm may carry a short editorial heading (e.g., “The Two Ways”). It is not part of the text, and it is never confused with a canonical superscription, which is always printed in italics.

9. Key-term glossary (Psalms; to be extended)

Each major term gets one primary rendering. If context forces a departure, give the Hebrew in a footnote.

Hebrew (Strong’s) Primary rendering Notes
ʾashre (H835) blessed (“How blessed…”) Exclamatory construct plural (“blessednesses of”). This word is distinct from baruk (H1288, “blessed” = spoken over by God or others). Use the footnote “Or happy.” Where both words occur close together, mark baruk in a footnote.
ḥesed (H2617) lovingkindness Covenant loyalty expressed in kindness. Use the same rendering every time. Footnote at its first occurrence in each psalm: “Heb ḥesed: loyal, covenant love.” (Decided by Brock, Nov 1 2026.)
nefesh (H5315) soul when it is the self as a whole being; life when life is at risk; throat/appetite when it is physical Footnote “Heb nephesh” whenever the rendering is not “soul.” Use “myself” only with a footnote.
torah (H8451) law Footnote “Heb torah, lit. instruction, teaching” wherever that sense matters. (Decided by Brock, Nov 1 2026.)
rashaʿ (H7563) wicked Consistent throughout.
tsaddiq (H6662) righteous Consistent throughout.
ḥattaʾ (H2400) sinners
lets (H3887) mockers Or “scoffers.” The word means people who deride and make light of wisdom.
hagah (H1897) meditate The word can denote low vocal sound (murmur, mutter, moan, growl). Add a footnote where that nuance matters.
ʾemunah (H530) faithfulness
ʾemet (H571) truth or faithfulness, depending on context Add a footnote when the word is paired with ḥesed.
mishpat (H4941) judgment (the act or verdict) or justice (the principle)
tsedeq / tsedaqah (H6664/6666) righteousness
yeshuʿah (H3444) salvation Use “deliverance” where the context is military, and add a footnote.
sheʾol (H7585) Sheol (transliterated)
ḥasid (H2623) faithful one / godly Related to ḥesed. Add a footnote.
ʿanaw / ʿani (H6035/6041) humble / afflicted
kavod (H3519) glory
yareʾ (H3372) (fear of the LORD) fear Do not soften it to “respect.”
hallelu-yah Praise the LORD Footnote “Heb Hallelu Yah.”

10. Workflow per psalm

  1. Pull the WLC text and OSHB morphology for the psalm.
  2. Parse every word, then draft a literal rendering.
  3. Revise for English readability, following §3.
  4. Check key terms against §9, and record any new terms in the glossary.
  5. Write footnotes.
  6. Run a copyright check: compare the draft only against the Hebrew and the public-domain KJV/ASV. Rework any line whose wording seems to echo a modern copyrighted version beyond what the Hebrew forces.
